title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
description: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Vol
body: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause."We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue."This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step."We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing."Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing."I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

schema.headline: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC

title: Stephen Fleming suggests England coach should be English
description: New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, has suggested the national team should be led by someone from England.Fleming, who will take
body: New Zealander Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, has suggested the national team should be led by someone from England.Fleming, who will take charge of his first series in South Africa in December, is the latest overseas coach to lead the England men's team.Since 1999, only two Englishmen - Peter Moores (twice) and Chris Silverwood - have been in charge of the Test side, while Ashley Giles had a spell as white-ball coach.In the same time period England have been led by two Zimbabweans, in Duncan Fletcher and Andy Flower, and Australian Trevor Bayliss - while Fleming has succeeded his fellow Kiwi Brendon McCullum, who remains white-ball coach. Another Australian, Matthew Mott, also had time in charge of the white-ball team.Fleming's backroom team, announced last week, is heavily weighted towards homegrown coaches.Former England opener Marcus Trescothick, who was in interim charge of the Test team earlier this year, is joined by ex-England wicketkeeper James Foster and former spinner Richard Dawson.Jonathan Trott, an Ashes winner with England, is about to begin a spell in charge of England Lions. Both Trott and Dawson were in the running for the Test job before Fleming was appointed.Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former New Zealand captain Fleming said it will be a "priority" of his tenure to help develop English coaches."I do believe that primarily the national team should be coached by a national representative," said Fleming."I'm grateful for the opportunity, but there will be some development in terms of the coaching, and you can see by our staff."As well as Fleming and McCullum filling the head coach roles for the men's national teams, England's selector, Marcus North, is Australian.In September it was announced that another Australian, Leah Poulton, will become the managing director of England women. Between 2020 and 2023 England women's head coach was Lisa Keightley, the former Australia international.In addition to developing the coaches on his own staff, Fleming said he will also occasionally invite county coaches and former England players into the set-up."There are some really key people who have come back into the system and I'm really pleased about that," he said."I look forward to working with them, but it is a real focus and it's an ambition as well that you will also get county coaches who will be introduced at certain times and you will get past players that will be asked to come back as well."It's really inclusive and a comfortable nature of using what's around, but also driving what should be driven within the county game and the English game."One of the criticisms of McCullum's four-year spell in charge of the Test team was his lack of time spent around the county game.In September, Fleming visited some counties and also spoke of his affection for the domestic game in England. The former batter had spells as a player with Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Middlesex.He confirmed he will spend part of next summer watching county cricket in the build-up to the home Ashes series."Yep, I'll be around and I really enjoyed this year getting to catch up," said Fleming. "A lot of the guys I played with are now in positions either coaching or the head positions at counties."It was good to catch up with those guys and get a feel for where the county game is at. I really enjoyed it and it will be a key part to continuing developing players."Fleming was appointed in July, though did not take charge for the series against Pakistan in August and September, meaning his first series at the helm will be the three matches in South Africa in December and January.The squad for that series is due to be named in the first week of November.England did not pick a specialist spinner in any of the three Tests against Pakistan, instead fielding four frontline seamers.In South Africa's ongoing Test against Australia in Gqeberha, the tourists have omitted Nathan Lyon despite the off-spinner sitting sixth on the all-time list of Test wicket-takers with 573.Last week, Shoaib Bashir was named as the only specialist red-ball spinner on England's list of fully centrally contracted players, while Mason Crane and Liam Patterson-White were given development deals.Following the tour of South Africa, spin will play a big role on the two-Test tour of Bangladesh in February.Asked if Bashir's contract means he is England's number-one spinner, Fleming said the Derbyshire man represents "continuity"."I acknowledge there's a raft of spinners just below that, that at times are putting their hand up," said Fleming."There is a raft of spinners there and are probably looking for an opportunity, and finding those conditions, it could be Bangladesh, where there could be two or three that will come along."The team could look quite different and that's the horses for courses example."But Bashir has got some experience and is still very young. There's an aspect of still looking and developing, and trying to find that right combination in the spin department."

title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
description: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by
body: Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised. In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby. The charge was eventually dropped.Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat."These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."The new rules will give drivers:a guaranteed 5 minute period to decide whether to parkA 10 minute window to leave without facing a penaltyCancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parksCancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machinesMaximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parkingA freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of PracticeOperators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge. Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament. The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice". The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

schema.headline: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules

title: Spurs 3-1 Coventry: James Maddison shines on Tottenham return
description: Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psych
body: Roberto de Zerbi has used all the tools at his disposal to discover the missing spark in struggling Tottenham Hotspur, from acting as an amateur psychologist to team bonding dinners, then a sunshine break in Marbella.The answer, at least when Spurs finally moved off the bottom of the table with their first Premier League win this season against Coventry City, came in the shape of James Maddison as he made his first start in 18 months.He missed most of last season after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in pre-season, before fracturing his shoulder in the opening-weekend defeat at Brentford in this campaign.The 29-year-old finally made it back into the Spurs starting line-up to face Coventry - and delivered in spectacular style to set them on the way to a 3-1 victory that De Zerbi hopes will finally give their season lift-off.Maddison could barely keep the smile from his face as he warmed up, then made his mark in the 14th minute by showing what Spurs have been missing with a brilliant right-foot finish from 20 yards, taking Mohammed Kudus' pass first time to arc a sweeping strike high beyond Coventry City keeper Carl Rushworth.It was a moment of sweet relief for Maddison, the goal getting loud gasps of admiration from Spurs supporters as it was shown several times on the stadium's big screens.Even though the goal came against his former club, Maddison celebrated with his trademark imaginary dart throwing motion before kissing the badge on his Spurs shirt.Maddison's significance to Spurs is illustrated by the fact they had won just 12 out of 57 Premier League games since his last top-flight goal, in a 1-0 victory against Manchester United in February 2025. They had averaged less than a point a game since then.And since his last start, at Liverpool on 27 April 2025, Spurs had won only 11 of 49 league games in between, losing 23.Spurs cannot kid themselves that this was a glorious victory. It was actually only their sixth win in the past 37 home league games - drawing 10 and losing 21 - and just their fourth league victory overall in 2026, having played 27, drawn 10 and lost 13.And it was the first time they scored three goals or more at home in the league since the opening day of last season, when they beat Burnley 3-0 in Thomas Frank's first game in charge.There are still too many nerves around Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and in De Zerbi's team for calm and relaxation.The victory margin flattered them somewhat, with Jack Rudoni equalising for Coventry City before Omar Marmoush's strike for his first goal for the club, then another from Ben Davies in stoppage time after a dreadful Rushworth error finally allowed Spurs to enjoy the relief of victory.And there were other things to celebrate. As well as Maddison's successful return to the starting line-up, there was the sight of Dejan Kulusevski finally back as an 87th-minute replacement for Kudus after 526 days out with a knee injury.Maddison got a deserved standing ovation when he was substituted for Conor Gallagher after 69 minutes, but the reception for Kulusevski was arguably even more rapturous as he finally took to the pitch again after such a long battle to regain fitness.It was Maddison, however, who claimed the major plaudits after he was the driving force behind the win that has proved so elusive - his positive approach playing with a smile on his face provides refreshment of its own after such a depressing sequence of results.He was eager to get on the ball, was constantly probing and prompting, all before he inevitably tired after the break."I spoke to the gaffer this weekend about it, feeling like it was the right moment for me to go back into the starting XI after a bit of a stop-start start to the season," Maddison told Sky Sports."I just wanted to play well and show my abilities, show what the team has missed the last 18 months. The gaffer asked me to play and wanted to enjoy watching from the side. Hopefully I did that, and a goal is always nice."If his aim was to show what Spurs have been missing, this was very much mission accomplished.And as well as Maddison and Kulusevski, Marmoush will gain confidence from his strike, another superb curling effort that gave Rushworth no chance.De Zerbi will know this is only a start, with a tough trip to face Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening (17:30 BST).He welcomed the return of Maddison and Kulusevski, saying: "They are different players, different talents, different personalities. With them in the dressing room there is a different atmosphere."What changes the atmosphere in the dressing room and beyond most are victories.Now De Zerbi and Spurs can actually build on three points at last, and the sights of Maddison and Kulusevski back in action will have the Italian hoping they can accelerate an improvement after the misery of recent times.

schema.headline: Spurs 3-1 Coventry: James Maddison shines on Tottenham return

title: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about
description: Image source, Monica ThomasImage caption, Monica is the founder of charity Women's Health Hope ByEmily HoltThis report contains detailed descriptions
body: Image source, Monica ThomasImage caption, Monica is the founder of charity Women's Health Hope ByEmily HoltThis report contains detailed descriptions of medical symptoms.Monica Thomas was in her teens when she started experiencing intimate itching and soreness, but despite numerous trips to the doctors it was dismissed as thrush.Her symptoms got worse, with sores and blisters leaving her in constant pain."I was bed bound for quite a long time because I couldn't walk," she says.Monica says she was examined 28 times in six months before being offered a biopsy.She says "we don't really talk about" gynaecological health as a society so there is a taboo around speaking about symptoms. "Even when we go to the doctors, for me, the embarrassment of having to get undressed...with these doctors looking it is embarrassing," she says."But equally when you're in pain or it's itching and you've got discomfort, living with it is just as bad."The 34-year-old from Suffolk was eventually diagnosed with a condition called lichen sclerosus. Image source, Dr Nighat ArifImage caption, Dr Nighat Arif is author of The Knowledge: Your guide to female health – from menstruation to the menopauseThe lifelong inflammatory condition affects genitals and can cause white patches to form with itching, soreness, splitting and tears, says Dr Nighat Arif, a GP specialising in women's health.It affects men and women but is more common in women over 50, external. There is also a small risk of vulval cancer., external"It's very sore to have sexual intercourse, to pass urine and it gets mixed up with sexually transmitted diseases but it's not contagious," she tells BBC Radio 5 Live podcast That Time of the Month. Research into the prevalence of vulval lichen sclerosus is limited but analysis by the University of Bristol of people in the West Midlands and Warwickshire estimated it affects about 1% of women. Dr Sophie Rees, who helped conduct the research, tells the BBC: "This is almost certainly an underestimate, as we know that there is often a very long delay to diagnosis, and some people probably go their entire lives undiagnosed."There is unfortunately a lot of shame and embarrassment around seeking help for vulval symptoms, as well as a lack of awareness, even amongst healthcare professionals."She adds: "More research is badly needed into true prevalence."'Lonely, horrific time'Monica says multiple misdiagnoses had a "significant" impact on her mental health."I didn't know how to go on... with having no answer, it was just a horrific,  lonely time."She was given medication for herpes. "I was very upset in an appointment with a dermatologist who got quite angry with me because I was like, 'it's not that'. "Then she said that she wanted me to have blood tests for HIV."Doctors told her she was "too young" to have lichen sclerosus."But sadly, women do have it at all ages, you can have it as a child. So I found that really quite difficult, but I always knew that it wasn't right."That Time of the Month What is lichen sclerosus? Listen now. Monica believes there should be more support for those with lichen sclerosus."Once you have a diagnosis, you're still necessarily not treated in the manner that you should, I don't even get a checkup," she says."I manage it on my own with my steroid cream and hope that I'm doing everything right." According to the NHS website,, external the cause of lichen sclerosus is unknown. It might be caused by the immune system mistakenly attacking and damaging your skin. It is not contagious, caused by an infection or by poor personal hygiene. Rubbing or damage to the skin can trigger the condition or make it worse. Image source, Clare BaumhaeurImage caption, Clare urged anyone with any symptoms to make sure they were examined by a doctorClare Baumhaeur, 53, from Kent first experienced symptoms aged five. "I was itchy and I was sore, and I was always told off, I wasn't obviously aware what was going on." Her symptoms worsened into adulthood with tears, blisters and sores."But you don't see other vulvas, so I had no idea mine wasn't normal. I'd had in that time eight smear tests as well and nothing was ever said."In 2016 Clare experienced a tear which did not heal. "I was 43 that year, having it for 38 years at that point, I just couldn't take it any more." A GP told Clare she had herpes and to go to a sexual health clinic, she says she was "shocked" as she had been married for 25 years.  She was eventually referred for a biopsy and was diagnosed with lichen sclerosus and vulval cancer. 'I'd never heard of it'"I'd never heard of lichen sclerosus and also I had a cancer that I'd ever heard of in a place I'd never heard of. "That was the first time I heard the word vulva, no health professional had mentioned it, so it was a lot to take in at that time."Clare had been in remission from vulval cancer for seven years, when a regular check-up revealed a cancer recurrence and she underwent surgery three years ago.In June another check up found pre-cancerous cells and she had a sixth surgery.Clare believes if she had been diagnosed with lichen sclerosis earlier, her cancer may have been diagnosed before it got to stage three."I had to have radiotherapy twice and that's left me with instant early menopause, lymphoedema and nerve damage."Monica encourages women experiencing any changes to their body to keep a diary."It's really important that we get to know our bodies better, to know what's normal for you in your private parts as well, because actually our vulvas do change."If you are being dismissed, get multiple opinions, just keep going back because you don't have to live without answers."She recommended the Lichen Sclerosus Guide, external which has a diagram and template to help you talk to doctors.

schema.headline: I have a condition people are too embarrassed to talk about

title: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya
description: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered me
body: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil".Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece".One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said.One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said.Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November.He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country.Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie."I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court."All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day."Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old.""We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside."The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned."My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover."My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said."I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced."I still love him and he is still my pastor."In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder."He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict.

schema.headline: Shakahola cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of 191 murder charges in Kenya

title: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row
description: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahas
body: The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.The Simpsons' Apu: 'A stereotype hiding in plain sight'The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient.Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."Speaking to Variety, external ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink."But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026."It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar - who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show - taking over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.In Apu's haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on French electro duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents.A year on he returns to wreak his revenge.Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes off his helmet and reveals himself to be Apu.He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick."I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.Just as he is about to set the city hall ablaze, Marge Simpson - serving as a thinly-veiled mouthpiece for the producers - intervenes, telling him: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing."Her famous bratty son Bart adds: "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do."Bart's father Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, reminding viewers of how important Apu has been to the town."You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands," said Homer."We took you for granted. I took you for granted."The episode will be made available for viewers in the UK to watch on Disney+ next week.

schema.headline: The Simpsons: Apu returns with new voice after race row

body: Depending on the contract you have, data charges may apply for accessing the internet on your mobile device.If you are not sure about the potential charges, please ask your mobile network provider. title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
description: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory fe
body: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.He was briefed by federal police – whose counter-terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."Witnesses saw the suspect do a U-turn before striking the MP and then reversing to ram her again, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said.Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese has been emotional when he has spoken about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year."We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds."We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life."This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.In the wake of the attack, a range of MPs have described wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.Women in politics are particularly scared, said Victorian state MP Georgie Purcell, who shares part of her electorate with Haines."Being a woman in politics changes the way you move through the world. We consider where we park our cars, the route we drive home, if we hold public events," she said in a statement."For many of us, the news... is our worst nightmare".Coalition Senator James Paterson told News24: "I'd like to say that I was surprised… but I'm not at all surprised."There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night."Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said."I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

schema.headline: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car

title: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape
description: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and t
body: Warning - this report contains graphic contentA woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand at a bar told the police "I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there" while the attack was taking place.In a 2023 video interview with an officer shown to the jury at his trial, the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009.The woman told the Southwark Crown Court jury the "lad culture" of the 2000s stopped her from reporting the TV star.She has accused Brand of grabbing her breasts at the bar in Soho in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet and allegedly raping her.The pair had been attending a birthday party when the alleged incidents happened.She said she waited two decades to come forward to the police because the thought of doing so "terrified" her.She said his celebrity status meant "it would be his word against mine"."I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends."The complainant worked for MTV at the time and said she was often surrounded by famous people.From behind a blue screen in the witness box she said times had changed.In those days - she said - "you weren't believed as a woman and it was a lad culture of 'you wearing this, so you were asking for it' and all that rubbish you were told back then".The complainant recalled Brand's "big weird grin" which she compared to the face of a clown as he allegedly launched forward and grabbed hold of her.Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested during cross examination that Brand and the woman went to the toilet consensually for a "kiss and a cuddle", but they abandoned the attempt to have a sexual encounter because of the filthy state of the flooded toilet.The woman, who became tearful while giving evidence, has rejected this version of events.She said she felt "dazed" after the alleged attack.Pressed on her claim of being dragged into the toilets against her will, the defendant's barrister suggested it would have been "perfectly easy" for her to have struggled or asked for help.She said she did not agree because he had been holding her quite strongly, saying "part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here".She described feeling numb and ashamed afterwards.She told the jury she had later confided in a friend, telling them Brand had  "tried to do it" - but held back from saying he had "succeeded" in raping her.The woman told the prosecution barrister that she didn't even know at the time that the alleged oral attack would be legally considered as rape.Earlier on Monday, the jury was shown a 2023 video interview with an officer in which the woman said she had been speaking to Brand about him hosting the Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth when he allegedly sexually assaulted her.In her recorded interview with police, the woman said "he literally just grabbed my boobs out of nowhere in the middle of the conversation, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs".A short while later, she said he "dragged me in the toilets" where the floor was flooded, before "he unzipped himself" and allegedly orally raped her.She said the alleged rape was "swift", and left her "in disbelief and shock"."The toilets were behind where he stood. It was literally just grab and pull. He was holding me quite strongly on the arm and pulled me in that direction," she said."Part of me was saying just get it over with so you can get out of here"."I just closed my eyes and tried not to be there. I just remember it felt like a force. I definitely said I don't want to do this," she added.After the alleged rape, the woman, who was in her 20s at the time, said Brand "turned to me and said 'oh I guess we should swap numbers now', like it was just all normal, like he hadn't just forced me to do that."Brand denies all the charges he faces.He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks.

schema.headline: Woman says she 'closed eyes and tried not to be there' during alleged Russell Brand rape

title: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos
description: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca Mo
body: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moonFigure caption, Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from JapanByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science  A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth. The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth. "I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon."The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained."But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity,  and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."Image source, NASAImage caption, Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formedThe rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g."It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.   "However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science.  So it's worth every gram," she said.Image source, JAXAImage caption, The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of PhobosScientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.There are two competing ideas.Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity."When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell."It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs."One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell."And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."Image source, Kevin Church/BBC NewsImage caption, Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum  Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

schema.headline: Japan's MMX mission set to grab a piece of Mars's moon Phobos

title: Cristiano Ronaldo given 30-day suspension by Portuguese FA
description: Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) after leaving his country'
body: Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and fined 255 euros (£215) by the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) after leaving his country's international camp last month. The 41-year-old captain walked out of Portugal's Nations League squad in September after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark on 1 October. Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement he had left because Portugal coach Jorge Jesus twice "broke his word", accusing him of an "absolute breach of trust".The Al-Nassr forward's suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will not miss any Portugal matches.Portugal face Denmark in the Nations League again on 14 November before travelling to Wales three days later.The FPF disciplinary committee said it took into account "the remorse shown" by Ronaldo in his statement, as well as his "contributions to soccer and recognition for athletic merit".It added that the forward submitted his CV, including his awards and achievements, as part of his defence. Ronaldo also referred the committee to his earlier statement, where he accepted accountability and apologised to his team-mates and fans for his actions, before adding he deserved to be punished.Portugal boss Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but has left the door open for his return.Pedro Proenca, president of the FPF, told Portuguese outlet Record there is a "strong desire" to have Ronaldo back with the national team once the matter is resolved.The five-time Ballon d'Or winner has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both men's world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the two Nations League titles.He joined Saudi Arabian side Al-Nassr in December 2022 on a reported annual salary of £177m and signed a contract extension last year.

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo given 30-day suspension by Portuguese FA

title: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra
description: Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.The make-up mogul s
body: Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer.The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model.The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel.Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media". "Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat. Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters. However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know"."Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says.  "They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done."British model Summer Nesbeth tells Newsbeat that she feels Victoria's Secret choosing Jenner was their attempt to keep up with young fans."She's an influencer with a lot of power and we are in the social media age," says the 25-year-old, who has walked the runway at New York Fashion Week.The lingerie brand's catwalk show was scrapped after its 2018 edition drew low ratings, as well as criticism that it was sexist, outdated and lacked diversity.It returned in 2024,  with a promise to "celebrate all women" and featured more a diverse range of talent, including Ashley Graham's appearance as a plus-sized model.Victoria's Secret created this year's Fantasy Bra in collaboration with jewellery brand Jacob & Co, who said it was the "most valuable" one ever created and took 15 artists more than 1,000 hours to create.Nesbeth believes the focus on the bra shows "how detached we are"."People can't eat, people can't afford to keep their lights on," she says. "I think there's a lot of things to say about where we're focussing our attention and where we're putting our money." BBC Newsbeat has contacted Victoria's Secret.

schema.headline: Kylie Jenner makes Victoria Secret debut in $50 million bra

title: Sarina Wiegman contract: Why England manager faces biggest challenge yet
description: Wiegman's successful England teams have been built on a core group of players from an outstanding generation - but a few cracks have appeared this yea
body: Wiegman's successful England teams have been built on a core group of players from an outstanding generation - but a few cracks have appeared this year.Seven of the team that started against world champions Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - and their 4-0 defeat in Mallorca laid bare the gap England must bridge to the world's best.That result also consigned England to two rounds of play-offs to reach next summer's World Cup.Beating Greece this month navigated the first of those, with games against Ukraine, who they have beaten twice already in 2026, to come before Christmas.Nevertheless, finding successors to those who have spearheaded the success will not be straightforward.Defensive stalwarts Lucy Bronze and Alex Greenwood will be 37 and 36 respectively by Euro 2029, while Leah Williamson and Keira Walsh will be 32.Other key players such as Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway will also have turned 30, far from past their best, but still a consideration."We have to continue the evolution of the Lionesses," record goalscorer Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast. "We can't stay stagnant or keep trying to win in the same ways all the time."Former England goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis thinks one of Wiegman's strengths as a manager is her willingness to give young players a chance. "She's not afraid of bringing in players who have never been capped before," Brown-Finnis told BBC Radio 5 Live. "Wiegman is looking right across the spectrum and asking who's on form, who can add to my squad, who can fill a position or a couple of different positions?" Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club, former Lionesses captain Steph Houghton said: "You can see Wiegman is trying to change a few things. The last camp she brought on Lexi Potter for her debut and she is now starting regularly for Chelsea. As a young player you need that to thrive in this environment."She is seeing the progress of young players coming through to press those who have been in the squad for a long time."It is not as though Wiegman has ignored squad regeneration.During her time in charge, she has handed debuts to 24 players, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.Those games against Greece offered a clue to her next steps.In Crete, Manchester City's Laura Blindkilde Brown, 23, showed glimpses of her ball-playing ability, while in the second leg 20-year-old Chelsea academy graduate Potter impressed in midfield.London City's Freya Godfrey, 21, and talented 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson also got their first caps as Wiegman scrutinised her options.Figures earlier this season showed the number of homegrown starters has been dropping in the Women's Super League (WSL) over the past four campaigns, with the league's growing prestige attracting more foreign stars.The Football Association (FA) chief football officer Dan Ashworth said Wiegman has helped bring "a golden age for women's football in this country".To prolong it, she will need to keep producing fruit from increasingly arid ground.Prior to Wiegman's appointment, England women had performed well at major tournaments - finishing third at the World Cup in 2015 and fourth in 2019 - but winning Euro 2022 was something new.WSL attendances rocketed, media coverage surged and clubs amplified their women's teams. However, four years on, there is evidence to suggest interest has plateaued.Initial crowd figures for the 2026-27 season are down on previous campaigns, while only 18,587 fans watched England beat Greece 5-0 at King Power Stadium, nearly 10,000 fewer than qualifiers at Nottingham Forest's City Ground and Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium this year.With so much competition, Lionesses success is crucial for sustaining momentum in the women's game - but expectations are higher now.A fanbase was born from success and has become accustomed to it. Will they tolerate anything less than finals and trophies?After all, Spain, Japan and hosts Brazil are among the many nations that look poised to have a significant say at the World Cup next summer.

schema.headline: Sarina Wiegman contract: Why England manager faces biggest challenge yet

title: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
description: French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country.P
body: French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country.Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre.Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.Earlier Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but they have since escalated to take in a broader range of concerns, with numbers at demonstrations this weekend bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.More than 2,500 people have been arrested, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews "where they need", without specifying which cities where they would be enforced.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage, and the funding would be recovered from those behind the violence."There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay," Lecornu said.He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work as a result of the riots and looting.Meanwhile, Nuñez said 200 investigators were analysing CCTV footage to try to identify possible ringleaders.He attempted to resign on Sunday, but Macron refused "given the need for continued command of law enforcement", the Élysée Palace said. The statement said Nuñez should be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings".More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) says.Its head Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that damage from the riots was estimated at "hundreds of millions of euros". Jean-Luc Chauvin, the president of the CCI's Marseille branch, told the BBC that many of the city's shop owners were in "deep distress" and fear for their survival.Looted goods have been listed on certain selling platforms, two French government ministers said. A Vinted spokesperson said the sale or solicitation of stolen goods was "strictly prohibited"."Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," it said.Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets over the weekend for protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.In the central city of Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing as the flames took hold.The US Embassy in France has issued an alert advising its citizens to avoid areas affected by the recent demonstrations.The warning says to "exercise caution" if they find themselves close to large gatherings. China and Germany have issued similar warnings.Some politicians have accused the left-wing La France Insoumise party of playing a role in the violence, with Lecornu alleging in an earlier news conference that some groups "want to create chaos in our country up until the presidential elections".The party's leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who will stand in next year's presidential election, responded by calling for the French PM to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".

schema.headline: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
